Shifting the axis to the edge needs the **parallel-axis theorem**.
**Step 1 — state the theorem.**
I = I_cm + **Md²** ✓
where d is the distance between the two parallel axes.
**Step 2 — identify the quantities.**
I_cm = **2 kg m²** (given, about the centre)
M = **1 kg**
d = the radius, **2 m**, since the new axis passes through the edge ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
I = 2 + (1)(2)²
= 2 + 4
= **6 kg m²** ✓
**Why the moment of inertia must increase.** The centre of mass is the axis about which
the moment of inertia is **least** ✓ Moving the axis anywhere else always adds the
positive term Md², and here it triples the value.
**A check on the given I_cm.** For a disc, I_cm = ½MR² = ½(1)(4) = **2 kg m²** ✓
exactly as stated - so the data are internally consistent.
**Why the theorem works.** Expanding Σm_i r_i² about the new axis gives the moment
about the centre **plus** Md², the cross term vanishing because the centre of mass is
by definition at the origin of the r_i ✓
**The condition for using it.** The two axes must be **parallel**, and one must pass
through the **centre of mass** ✓ The theorem cannot be used to go directly between two
arbitrary axes - one must route through the centre.
**The companion theorem.** The **perpendicular-axis theorem**, I_z = I_x + I_y, applies
only to **plane laminae** ✓ For this disc, the moment about a diameter is
I_d = I_cm/2 = **1 kg m²**, since the two diameters are equivalent and must sum to 2.
**A worked variation.** About a **tangent in the plane** of the disc:
I = I_diameter + MR² = 1 + 4 = **5 kg m²** ✓
About a tangent **perpendicular** to the plane: 2 + 4 = **6 kg m²** ✓ our case.
**Why it matters.** Rotating a body about an off-centre axis makes it far harder to
spin up ✓ which is why a door is hinged at its edge but a flywheel is mounted through
its centre.
**Reading the distractors.** **4 kg m²** ✗ is the Md² term alone, forgetting I_cm.
**8 kg m²** ✗ and **10 kg m²** ✗ would need d² of 6 and 8 ✓
∴ 6 kg m².

The ratio of magnetic moment to angular momentum is the **gyromagnetic ratio**,
**e/2m**.
**Step 1 — write the magnetic moment of the orbiting electron.** An electron circling
with period T constitutes a current
I = e/T = ev/(2πr) ✓
so its magnetic moment is
µ = IA = [ev/(2πr)](πr²) = **evr/2** ✓
**Step 2 — write the angular momentum.**
L = m v r ✓
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
µ/L = (evr/2)/(mvr)
= **e/2m** ✓
**Why the orbit radius and speed cancel.** Both appear as the product **vr** in each
quantity ✓ So the ratio is the same for **every** orbit - the first, the second, any of
them. The question's "1st orbit" is a red herring, included to see whether that is
recognised.
**The name and value.**
**gyromagnetic ratio** = e/2m = **8·8 x 10¹⁰ C kg⁻¹** ✓
**The Bohr magneton.** Combining with the quantisation L = nℏ:
µ = (e/2m)(nℏ) = n **µ_B**, with
µ_B = eℏ/2m = **9·27 x 10⁻²⁴ A m²** ✓
the natural unit of atomic magnetism, and the magnitude of the magnetic moment of the
n = 1 orbit.
**Why the moment and the angular momentum point opposite ways.** The electron's charge
is **negative**, so the conventional current circulates **against** its motion ✓ Hence
µ̄ = −(e/2m)L̄, and atomic magnetic moments are antiparallel to their angular momenta.
**The surprise of electron spin.** For **spin** angular momentum the ratio is
**e/m**, twice the orbital value ✓ The extra factor - the **g-factor**, close to 2 - was
unexplained until Dirac derived it from relativistic quantum mechanics, and its tiny
deviation from exactly 2 is the most precisely tested prediction in all of physics.
**Where the ratio is used.** In the **Larmor precession** of a magnetic moment in a
field, ω = (e/2m)B ✓ and so in NMR, MRI and electron spin resonance.
**Reading the distractors.** **e/m** ✗ is the **spin** ratio, twice too large. **2m/e**
✗ and **m/e** ✗ are reciprocals ✓ A dimensional check - C kg⁻¹ - eliminates both.
∴ e/2m.

**Mass is invariant**; it is the **weight** that changes from one world to another.
**Step 1 — distinguish the two quantities.**
**mass** - the amount of matter, a **scalar**, measured in kilograms ✓ an intrinsic
property of the body
**weight** - the gravitational **force** on it, mg, a **vector** in newtons ✓ depending
on where the body is
**Step 2 — apply this on the Moon.** The body is the same body, so its mass is still
**M** ✓
**Step 3 — note what does change.** The Moon's surface gravity is about **g/6**, so the
**weight** falls to Mg/6 ✓ The astronaut who can lift 60 kg on Earth can lift 360 kg on
the Moon - but those 360 kg are still 360 kg of matter.
**Why the Moon's g is a sixth.** From g = GM/R²:
the Moon's mass is **1/81** of Earth's
its radius is **0·27** of Earth's, so R² is 0·0745 ✓
g_moon/g_earth = (1/81)/0·0745 = **0·166 ≈ 1/6** ✓
**How mass is measured in weightlessness.** Not with a balance, which needs gravity, but
by **oscillation** ✓ Astronauts strap into a spring-mounted chair and the period
T = 2π√(m/k) gives the mass. Mass has meaning even where weight does not.
**Why mass resists acceleration regardless.** F = ma holds everywhere ✓ Pushing a
heavy crate in orbit is just as hard as on Earth - it will not fall on your foot, but
it will still crush you if it drifts into you.
**The one caveat from relativity.** Mass does increase with speed, as m = m₀/√(1 − v²/c²)
✓ but that is a matter of **velocity**, not of location, and is utterly negligible at
any speed a spacecraft reaches.
**The everyday confusion.** Bathroom scales are marked in kilograms but measure
**force** ✓ Taken to the Moon, such a scale would read M/6 - which is where the first
distractor comes from, and it is a reading of **weight**, not of mass.
**Reading the distractors.** **M/6** ✗ is the Moon **weight** expressed in kilogram
units. **6M** ✗ reverses it, and **zero** ✗ confuses weightlessness with masslessness ✓
∴ M.

Bending the rod into a ring fixes the radius from the **length**, and then the two
moments of inertia can be compared.
**Step 1 — write the rod's moment of inertia.** About a perpendicular axis through its
centre, for a rod of length L:
**I = ML²/12** ✓
**Step 2 — find the ring's radius.** The same rod forms the circumference:
L = 2πr
**r = L/(2π)** ✓
**Step 3 — write the ring's moment of inertia about a diameter.**
**I′ = ½Mr²** ✓
(the perpendicular-axis theorem: about the central axis it is Mr², and the two diameters
share that equally)
= ½M(L/2π)²
= **ML²/(8π²)** ✓
**Step 4 — take the ratio.**
I/I′ = (ML²/12) ÷ (ML²/8π²)
= 8π²/12
= **2π²/3** ✓
**Step 5 — evaluate.** 2(9·87)/3 = **6·58** ✓ The straight rod has over six times the
moment of inertia of the ring about its diameter.
**Why the ring is so much easier to spin.** Bending the rod brings all its mass
**closer** to the axis ✓ The rod stretches out to L/2 on each side, whereas the ring's
radius is only L/2π = **0·159L** - less than a third as far.
**A check with numbers.** Take M = 1 kg and L = 1 m:
rod: I = 1/12 = **0·0833 kg m²**
ring: r = 0·159 m, I′ = ½(1)(0·0253) = **0·0127 kg m²** ✓
ratio **6·58** ✓ matching 2π²/3.
**Why the diameter and not the central axis.** About the **central** axis - the one
through the centre perpendicular to the ring's plane - the moment is **Mr²**, twice as
large ✓ The question specifies the diameter, which is the harder case and needs the
perpendicular-axis theorem.
**The perpendicular-axis theorem.** For a plane lamina, **I_z = I_x + I_y** ✓ For a
ring, I_z = Mr² and the two diameters are equivalent, so each is Mr²/2.
**Why the mass cancels.** It appears in both expressions ✓ and so does L² - leaving a
pure number built from π.
**Reading the distractors.** **3/2π²**, **8/3π²** and **5/3π²** ✗ all arise from
mis-handling the factor 8π² or from using Mr² instead of ½Mr² ✓
∴ 2/3 π².

Once both balls are in the air, the **only** external force on the system is gravity, so
the centre of mass accelerates at **g**.
**Step 1 — write Newton's second law for the system.**
M a_cm = **F_external** ✓
where M is the total mass. Internal forces, if any, cancel in pairs.
**Step 2 — identify the external force.** With air resistance neglected, the only one
is **gravity**:
F_ext = (m₁ + m₂)g ✓
**Step 3 — divide.**
a_cm = (m₁ + m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂)
= **g**, directed vertically downward ✓
**Why the masses cancel.** The gravitational force on each ball is proportional to its
own mass ✓ so the total force is proportional to the total mass, and the ratio is
simply g.
**Why the speeds and directions do not matter.** They determine where each ball
**goes**, but not the force on it ✓ A ball thrown up, one thrown sideways and one
dropped all accelerate downward at g - and so does their centre of mass.
**The remarkable consequence.** The centre of mass traces a **simple parabola**, exactly
as a single projectile would ✓ whatever complicated paths the individual balls follow.
**The firework illustration.** A rocket explodes into a hundred fragments flying in all
directions ✓ Yet the centre of mass of the debris continues along the **original
parabola** undisturbed, because the explosion's forces are all **internal**. It is one
of the most striking demonstrations in mechanics.
**Why internal forces never matter.** By Newton's third law they occur in equal and
opposite pairs and sum to zero ✓ A system cannot accelerate its own centre of mass -
which is also why one cannot lift oneself by one's own bootstraps.
**What would change the answer.** **Air resistance** ✓ It is external and depends on
each ball's speed and shape, so the centre of mass would then accelerate at **less**
than g, and the amount would depend on both balls' motions. The question's idealisation
is what makes the clean answer possible.
**The momentum statement of the same fact.** The total momentum changes at the rate
Mg ✓ regardless of how it is distributed between the two balls.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Depends on the masses**" ✗ - they cancel. "**Depends on
the speeds**" ✗ and "**on the directions**" ✗ - gravity is indifferent to both ✓
∴ is equal to g (Acceleration due to gravity).
